extracted.intended_audience: writers in film/television/radio/online media, researchers, and the general public interested in the Writers Guild of America
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards, rules, and practices used by the Writers Guild of America that affect how professional film/TV/radio/online writing is credited, registered, compensated, and governed. Useful for writers navigating membership, credits, compensation, and collective bargaining with studios/streamers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership eligibility by geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership in either WGAE or WGAW is generally contingent on geography: jobs west of the Mississippi River are represented by Writers Guild of America West (WGAW) and jobs east of the river by Writers Guild of America East (WGAE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a writer is eligible for union membership, the physical location of the job determines which guild represents that work. (Page notes jurisdictional examples such as Los Angeles and other production hubs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership transfer and good-standing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If a writer joins one guild and later moves across the Mississippi River, they are not required to transfer; membership transfer is optional. Members must remain in good standing (pay all outstanding dues, repay loans, etc.) with their original guild.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remaining in 'good standing' is explicitly required to retain membership and to be eligible for optional transfer between WGAE and WGAW.

rubrics_metrics.name: WGA screenwriting credit system (final arbiter role)
rubrics_metrics.description: The WGA screenwriting credit system is used to determine who receives credit for writing a film, television, theatrical, or other media work under the WGA's jurisdiction; the guilds are the final arbiters on who and how writers are listed in the credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit determinations are authoritative and binding within WGA jurisdiction — writers should use the guild process to resolve credit disputes rather than relying solely on producers/studios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit determines compensation and residuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The credit a writer receives is directly tied to their percentage of initial compensation and residuals for that project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtaining proper credit through the WGA system has direct financial consequences; disputes over credit can materially affect a writer's pay and residual entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: WGA script registration service (establishing date of creation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The WGA script registration service is run by both guilds to establish the date of creation of literary property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers can register scripts with the WGA to create an official record of creation date useful for protecting ownership/claims, though the page does not detail the registration process itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: WGA Awards recognition of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Writers Guild of America Awards are presented annually by both guilds in recognition of excellence in film, television, and radio writing, including both fiction and non-fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards are presented simultaneously on both coasts; the page notes the awards honor outstanding writing but does not list specific judging criteria on this page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration between writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Both guilds arbitrate between writers when conflicts arise (for example, credit disputes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WGA provides an internal arbitration mechanism to decide disputes among writers, reinforcing the guild's role as final arbiter on credit and related matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective bargaining objectives: residuals and pension/benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: WGA negotiations and strikes historically sought changes to compensation systems including first theatrical residuals, improved pensions, payment terms for pay TV, formulas for home video residuals, and residuals from syndicated reruns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical strike outcomes indicate the guild prioritizes securing residual structures and benefits for writers as media and distribution models evolve (theatrical, pay TV, home video, syndication). Examples: 1960 (first theatrical residuals), 1981 (pay TV), 1985 (home video formula), 1988 (syndicated rerun residuals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation and dispute focus on new media and streaming compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent disputes have included compensation and residuals for content made for new media, programs on DVD, streaming media, and the use of AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2007–08 and 2023 strikes are cited as involving new media/streaming/AI issues; writers should expect the guild to negotiate specific terms and licensing language for emerging distribution technologies and AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: WGA stance and bargaining over AI and AI-generated material
rubrics_metrics.description: The guilds have confronted the use of AI: the 2023 strike included disputes over residuals from the use of AI and streaming media; WGAE has publicly condemned use of AI-generated articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WGA actively seeks AI licensing language in contracts and has taken public positions opposing unlicensed AI-generated material; writers should rely on negotiated AI terms rather than ad-hoc use by employers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint bargaining and coordinated strike actions
rubrics_metrics.description: WGAE and WGAW negotiate contracts in unison and launch strike actions simultaneously; they operate independently but perform common activities such as negotiating contracts and launching strikes together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two coast guilds coordinate on major labor actions to increase negotiating leverage; writers should be aware that both guilds act together on national contract issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional coverage of production hubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Although historically centered in Los Angeles, production has expanded; some new production hubs (e.g., Albuquerque) remain under WGAW jurisdiction while other growing hubs (Chicago, Atlanta, New Orleans) are under WGAE jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers working outside traditional centers must check which guild's jurisdiction covers the production location, since jurisdiction affects membership, credits, and negotiated contract terms.
